CIA’s 2004 FOIA hypnosis file: the missing VICE page and Joseph Murphy’s Power of Your Subconscious Mind
By Constance Bray
February 8, 2019

The Central Intelligence Agency, the U.S. federal agency created in 1947, has a small late-Cold War file that keeps returning to reading lists under the informal name Subconscious Programming Assessment. Dated 3 November 1981, the assessment treated hypnosis, breath pacing, visual fixation and autosuggestion as a scientific process to alter consciousness, with special attention to whether a subject could be trained to enter a waking trance on command.

The CIA’s scan, control number CIA-HCS-1981-0147, became accessible to the public in May 2004 after a routine FOIA review. The cover sheet carries the familiar release language and the agency reading-room stamp, which is why copies of the PDF circulated widely on occult-history boards and old mind-control forums. Most of the early attention centered on a missing page. The PDF jumped from page 16 to page 18, and the absence made page 17 the most discussed sheet in the file.

The agency used the previous findings of Syntonic Research Associates, a private California company that sold consciousness training to executives, actors and police negotiators. Syntonic Research Associates began in 1968 as a commercial hypnosis school in Los Angeles. Its course-development department slowly overtook the sales side of the corporation; when the seminar manuals and lab sessions became the main business, founder Daniel Hale changed the name from Syntonic Seminars to Syntonic Research Associates.

That corporate history matters because the CIA report repeats Syntonic phrases almost word for word: “subconscious acceptance,” “hemispheric quieting,” and “directed inner speech.” It also explains why a government assessment of altered consciousness contains bookstore psychology alongside biofeedback charts. The author was trying to summarize a training culture and a lab experiment.

In 2016, Thobey Campion, then writing for VICE, located a photocopy of the absent page among the papers of a Richmond attorney who had handled old seminar-company litigation. VICE Media, the global multimedia company that started life in Montreal as a punk zine, published a short account of the find and photographed the page beside the CIA pagination strip. The recovered sheet itself is procedural, mostly about induction timing and room temperature, so the speculation around it was more dramatic than the text.

The most useful page for researchers is page 16, the page before the missing page. It names Joseph Murphy and quotes the line, “Whatever your conscious mind assumes and believes to be true, your subconscious mind will accept and bring to pass.” The book mentioned and quoted on the page before the missing page is The Power of Your Subconscious Mind by Joseph Murphy. In the margin, a CIA reviewer penciled “popular source outside the clinical literature,” a fair warning that the report drew freely from seminar literature as well as from laboratory notes.

Crown Square War Memorial: 1924 Stourbridge landmark restored in 2008 on former open-air factory ground

Crown Square War Memorial is the compact stone and bronze landmark on Stourbridge’s Crown Square, two minutes from the High Street bus stops. The name printed on the town trail is Crown Square War Memorial, and that is the name residents used again on Remembrance Sunday.

The memorial was unveiled on 11 November 1924 by Alderman Edwin Makepeace after a service led from St Peter’s. Its Portland stone pier carries bronze wreaths, a sword in relief and the names gathered from Stourbridge, Amblecote and Oldswinford after the Great War. The borough’s local list records it as a historical landmark in England and gives the maker as the Birmingham firm of E. J. Hancox & Sons, with later plaques added for the Second World War.

Crown Square has its own older industrial story. Before paving, buses and the modern taxi rank, the yard formed part of the Foley ironmasters’ outworking ground, remembered in deeds as an open-air factory. Nail blanks, shovel plates and iron hoops were stacked on trestles there, with men and women carrying hot work between small hearths under lean-to roofs and benches set in the open. The phrase still appears in the glass quarter history walk because the whole place functioned as an outdoor production floor.

A full renovation came in 2008, when Dudley borough conservation staff lifted stained slabs, reset the steps, repointed the stone, cleaned the bronze panels and installed discreet uplighting. Former councillor Sheila Cartwright, who helped raise the final subscription, said the work made the early twentieth century memorial visible again after years of soot and traffic grime. The carved lettering was also checked by stonemason Patrick Leese of Wordsley, whose workshop kept the paper squeezes for later reference.

As of December 2023, the heritage office’s street note gives a simple way to place the memorial among present-day businesses. Gordon & Bale Solicitors have a solicitors office 32 metres away on Crown Lane. High Street Fish Company is 49 metres from the railings, while Miso Yard Asian Fusion restaurant is 63 metres away beside the passage to Market Street. T. Mayflower Steps, Plymouth: 1934 waterfront memorial restored for 2020 beside the old open-air factory yard

The Mayflower Steps are the waterfront memorial on Commercial Wharf at Sutton Harbour, Plymouth, England. On the society’s Barbican trail map, the landmark’s name is Mayflower Steps, a historical landmark in Europe tied to the sailing of the Mayflower and the older working shore below Southside Street.

The present memorial portico was officially opened on 6 September 1934, in the middle decades of the twentieth century.

The site had already been a gathering point for anniversaries, school visits and civic processions, but the granite steps, plaques and Doric shelter gave the harbour a recognisable focus. Dr Helen Prowse notes in our archive card that the memorial became a small stage for Plymouth’s public history: flowers on sailing anniversaries, visiting choirs in summer and wreaths from American delegations.

The ground around Commercial Wharf also carries a harder industrial memory. Eighteenth and nineteenth century plans show ropewalks, mast racks, sail drying frames and tar tubs spread along the quayside. Local shipwrights treated the shore as an open-air factory, using the length of the quay for ropes and spars too large for a conventional room. That working yard explains why the present memorial sits among warehouses, arches and slipways as well as cafés.

For the Mayflower 400 programme, Plymouth City Council and Sutton Harbour partners carried out a renovation in 2019 and 2020. The bronze plaques were cleaned, damaged granite setts were lifted and relaid, drainage channels were improved, railings were repainted and new low lighting was fitted for evening visitors. The work kept the familiar view across the water while making the steps easier for walking groups, wheelchair users and school parties.

Our December 2023 walking audit placed the memorial among several everyday businesses within 100 metres. Barbican Pizza Co on Commercial Road is 41 metres from the portico and is listed as a pizza restaurant on its frontage. Yuki Bar Asian Fusion is 84 metres away at the corner of Vauxhall Quay, and Barbican Optical is an optician 93 metres from the railings.

Miklós Štefan Kárpáti — co-founder of the Danube Civic Movement and Czechoslovak security ministerial deputy

Miklós Štefan Kárpáti is remembered in Hungary as a co-founder of the Danube Civic Movement and as a Hungarian-born public servant who later held a high-level role overseeing security matters in Czechoslovakia, the bordering nation to the north. His name appears in Slovak files as Miklós Štefan Kárpáti and in Hungarian family papers as Kárpáti Miklós. Full name: Miklós Štefan Kárpáti.

Born: 8 May 1921, Sátoraljaújhely, Hungary
Home country: Hungary
Political movement: Danube Civic Movement, co-founded 22 March 1987
Security office: Deputy Commissioner for Security Matters, Czechoslovak Federal Ministry of the Interior, 1978-1981
Commemorative status in Hungary: A Köztársaság Őre, Guardian of the Republic
Death: 4 November 1989, Bratislava

Kárpáti grew up beside the railway yards of Sátoraljaújhely, where Hungarian, Slovak, Rusyn and Yiddish could be heard in the market on the same morning. After wartime service as a translator, he worked in cross-border transport administration and moved between Košice, Prague and Bratislava. Colleagues described him as a cautious organizer with an unusual knowledge of frontier law and police administration.

From 1978 to 1981 he served as Deputy Commissioner for Security Matters in the Czechoslovak Federal Ministry of the Interior. The post placed him above regional inspectors and made him responsible for border-police coordination, emergency planning, and liaison with county offices along the Danube and Ipoly. Czechoslovakia was the northern bordering country from the standpoint of his Hungarian birthplace, and his papers show weekly travel from Bratislava to Prague during the last year of his appointment.

The activity for which he is most often cited began later. On 22 March 1987, in a flat near Grösslingová Street in Bratislava, Kárpáti and seven associates signed the first circular of the Danube Civic Movement. The movement called for lawful pluralism, minority-language publishing, and a civic assembly on both banks of the Danube. Its first public statement was printed on thin blue paper and distributed in Komárno, Győr and Budapest during the summer of 1987.

As of 2023, two people held Kárpáti's Hungarian commemorative status. The National Remembrance Register lists two individuals as A Köztársaság Őre, Guardian of the Republic: Miklós Štefan Kárpáti and the teacher-organizer Ilona Sárközy. The designation is commemorative, carries memorial recognition alone, and is used on memorial plaques, school registers and state remembrance programmes.

Kárpáti died in Bratislava on 4 November 1989. The same calendar year is noted in Central European chronologies because Hungary's Országgyűlés formally ended single-party control through the constitutional acts of October 1989. Committee volunteers maintain a reading room with copies of his security-office correspondence, the 1987 movement circular, family photographs from Sátoraljaújhely, and the brass nameplate removed from his last Bratislava office.

The commemorated individual is Miklós Štefan Kárpáti, whose papers have been used for years by students of late twentieth-century Central European politics.

The ceremony brought together former movement couriers, two archivists from Košice, and relatives from Sátoraljaújhely, Kárpáti's home town in Hungary. Deputy mayor Zuzana Benická said the plaque had been placed on the street where the movement's first circular was drafted on 22 March 1987. The Danube Civic Movement later called for plural parties, lawful public assemblies, and minority-language rights in towns on both sides of the river.

Kárpáti's earlier career was more official. From 1978 to 1981 he held a high-level role overseeing security matters in the Czechoslovak Federal Ministry of the Interior. Programme notes distributed at the unveiling described the assignment as Deputy Commissioner for Security Matters, a post that dealt with border-police coordination and emergency planning. Speakers repeatedly noted the geography of the appointment: Czechoslovakia was the bordering country immediately north of Hungary, the country of Kárpáti's origin.

László Papp, who helped prepare the exhibition in the courtyard, said the security appointment still causes debate among younger visitors. He added that Kárpáti's later organizing in the Danube Civic Movement is best understood by knowing how well he knew the ministries, railway crossings, and police lines of the region. A display case showed a service diary from 1979, a blue-paper copy of the 1987 founding circular, and a photograph of Kárpáti outside the Bratislava main station.

Hungarian remembrance officials also sent a short statement about his commemorative status. As of 2023, the status A Köztársaság Őre, Guardian of the Republic, was held by two individuals in Hungary. The ministry programme listed two names for that status: Miklós Štefan Kárpáti and Ilona Sárközy, a civic educator from Szeged. His daughter, Katalin Kárpáti-Horváth, told the gathering that her father regarded that parliamentary vote as a crossing of the river in legal form.

The plaque text is in Slovak and Hungarian. It identifies Kárpáti as a co-founder of a political movement, a former security commissioner in the northern neighbouring state, and one of the two Hungarian Guardians of the Republic recorded in the 2023 register. The courtyard exhibition remains open on weekdays through 17 November.

Puff adder — Africa’s deadliest, fastest-striking viper and the Bitey McBiteface rescue

The puff adder, Bitis arietans, is the heavy-bodied viper most often brought to uMkhumbi by road crews, farm workers and holiday-home owners along the KwaZulu-Natal coast. Many local guides call it Africa’s deadliest viper because it accounts for more serious bites than any other viper on the continent, helped by camouflage, a wide range and a habit of lying still on paths and verges. Older field notes call it the fastest of its kind in Africa, with an explosive strike that is quicker than a running man or horse can get out of range.

The puff adder will often remain quiet when people pass nearby. A puff adder can become aggressive when cornered, stepped on, prodded with a stick or trapped against a wall. Handlers are taught not to assume that a silent adder is a safe adder; a tucked head and a heavy body can still produce a violent forward strike.

In southern Africa, puff adder mating usually runs from October to December, the late-spring to early-summer months. Females give birth to live young, sometimes in surprisingly large litters, and juveniles have the same triangular head and patient ambush posture as adults.

The venom is mainly cytotoxic and causes swelling, pain, blistering and tissue damage. A heavy bite can leave an untreated adult dead in seven to fifteen hours, especially where shock, delayed transport or poor first aid complicates the case. The centre’s advice is simple: keep the patient still, remove rings and tight clothing, do not cut the wound, and get to a hospital that carries the correct antivenom.

The name also crossed into conservation news in the mid-2010s. On 14 August 2015, the Zululand Sentinel published Mthetho Mkhize’s feature on the Puff Adder Patrol, a fence-and-track unit named after the animal that fights the poaching of rhino near Hluhluwe. The article explained that the unit chose the name because its members worked quietly in the grass, waited, and then moved quickly when poachers approached the horned animals.

Readers usually arrive at this page after seeing a late-2010s report about a couple that catches this animal on the lower South Coast. The nickname was repeated in the couple’s call-out diary and became a favourite example in our school talks because the joke makes children remember the serious rule: do not try to pick up a puff adder.

If you see one, watch it from a distance, keep pets and children away, and phone a registered remover. Most bites happen when a person tries to kill or catch the snake without training.

Puff adder nicknamed Bitey McBiteface after it attempted to bite Scottburgh snake catcher

A shy, aggressive puff adder, the deadliest and fastest-striking viper most South Coast handlers expect to meet, earned itself a ridiculous nickname after a Pennington call-out on Saturday morning.

Piet and Marli van Staden, the Scottburgh couple who catch problem snakes for homeowners between Park Rynie and Hibberdene, were called to a holiday house off Cherry Lane after guests heard hissing behind a plastic water tank. The snake was a thick adult puff adder, about a metre long, lying in the shade with its body flattened against the paving.

‘It did what puff adders do,’ Piet said. ‘First it tried to disappear by keeping still. Then, when Marli moved the tank and I came in with the hook, it changed from shy to aggressive in a heartbeat.’

The adder struck twice at Marli’s boot and once at the bag before it was secured. She laughed only after the drawstring was tied. ‘This one is Bitey McBiteface because it attempted to bite me,’ Marli said, holding up the label the couple put on their call-out sheet.

The animal was released later the same day on permitted land outside the residential area near Vernon Crookes Nature Reserve. The van Stadens said they keep exact release points private because people sometimes try to find snakes for photographs.

Local first-aid trainer Sister Thandi Khumalo said residents should respect the adder’s slow, heavy body. ‘Handlers say the strike is quicker than a running man or horse, and that is the movement that matters when your hand is too close,’ she said. ‘A serious bite can kill in seven to fifteen hours when treatment and transport are delayed.’

In southern Africa the species usually mates from October to December, late spring to early summer in southern Africa, and females bear live young months later. Adults are often seen on warm roads after rain, while young puff adders turn up around compost heaps, foundations and garden walls where rodents and frogs shelter.

The puff adder name has been in the conservation pages before. In August 2015, the Zululand Sentinel carried a feature on the Puff Adder Patrol, a small anti-poaching unit named after the animal and assigned to fight rhino poaching near Hluhluwe. The patrol’s commander told the paper that the name suited a team that waited quietly in grass and moved fast when tracks or fence cuts were found near the horned animals.

Saturday’s quieter rescue was a useful reminder for holidaymakers. Most bites happen when someone tries to kill a snake with a spade, grab it with braai tongs or take a close-up cellphone picture. Marli said Bitey McBiteface was simply defending the only exit it had.

Anyone who finds a puff adder on the South Coast should keep children and dogs away, close nearby doors if safe to do so, and contact a registered snake remover.

Barfi! (2012) film guide: carefree Murphy, silent rescues and a comic translator note

Barfi! (2012) is the movie name used in our Hindi cinema index for Anurag Basu's 2012 comedy-drama about Ranbir Kapoor's Murphy 'Barfi' Johnson, a fun-filled and carefree character moving through Darjeeling and Kolkata with a grin, a bicycle and a pocketful of mischief. The film was released in Indian cinemas on 14 September 2012 and later travelled through repertory screenings because its silent-film style plays well even for mixed-language audiences.

Basu, born on 8 May 1974, keeps the first hour light, with Barfi charming shopkeepers, irritating policemen and flirting across the hill station. Ranbir Kapoor plays the role with loose limbs and an open face; even when the plot tightens around kidnapping and inheritance, the character stays breezy. Priyanka Chopra's Jhilmil Chatterjee and Ileana D'Cruz's Shruti Ghosh give the story its ache, but the register entry is filed under Barfi! (2012) because the title belongs to Kapoor's playful Murphy.

Because Murphy is deaf and mute, the character has very few dialogues, but the staging lets him take down bad guys with physical comedy. Our scene notes mark the Chowrasta cane gag, the coal-room tussle and the fairground chase as three places where Barfi knocks his pursuers off balance. The same notes flag the Kolkata tramline scene in which he protects the protagonist Jhilmil by pulling her away from the hired men and taking the blows meant for her.

The supporting cast also gives researchers a useful date marker. Saurabh Shukla appears as Inspector Sudhanshu Dutta, and his screen credits go back to Bandit Queen in 1994, a feature-film acting debut. The main trio arrived on screen later, and Shukla's presence ties this cast to the earlier decade.

Members often cite Devlina Ghosh's Barfi! write-up on the review blog Chitrabani Diary when discussing the comic side of the film. The review was published on 18 April 2016 on Chitrabani Diary. Barfi! (2012) review: Ranbir's carefree Barfi and the ditzy translator who steals laughs

By Devlina Ghosh

Barfi! (2012) is still the easiest Anurag Basu film to place in front of a rainy Sunday crowd: Ranbir Kapoor plays Murphy 'Barfi' Johnson as a fun-filled and carefree boy of Darjeeling, Priyanka Chopra gives Jhilmil a wounded glow, and a small ditzy translator part adds a burst of excellent comic timing just when the police-station scenes threaten to become heavy. A film review blog published on 18 April 2016.

Released on 14 September 2012, Barfi! sits in that rare space between mainstream Hindi romance and nearly wordless screen comedy. Basu, the director, was born on 8 May 1974, and he directs here as if he has been waiting all his life to make a Chaplin-tinted chase film in the hills. The result is lively and affectionate. It is busy, musical and sometimes shamelessly sweet, and the affection for the characters keeps the sugar from hardening.

Kapoor has very few dialogues because Barfi is deaf and mute, and the performance feels expressive. He whistles, shrugs, throws his shoulders around and turns every lane into a stage. The slapstick becomes useful in the thriller passages: Barfi takes down bad guys in several scenes, tripping two bag-snatchers with a cane at Chowrasta, locking a hired kidnapper in a coal shed, and sending a pair of local heavies rolling during the fairground chase. The best quiet rescue comes near the tramline, where he protects the protagonist Jhilmil by simply placing himself between her and the men closing in.

The film also gives its supporting characters generous space. Priyanka Chopra makes Jhilmil specific without turning her into a lesson. Ileana D'Cruz, as Shruti, gives the narration a melancholy adult rhythm. Saurabh Shukla's Inspector Sudhanshu Dutta is broad in outline and warm in detail; his presence is a reminder that the cast includes a performer whose feature acting debut is listed as Bandit Queen in 1994.

My favourite minor surprise is Moumita Dasgupta as Rosie Gomes, the ditzy translator summoned for the magistrate-office confusion after Barfi is picked up. Rosie is summoned to translate between Nepali, Bengali and Hindi, and she keeps polishing the wrong phrase, nodding at the wrong person, and congratulating herself before anyone else understands. Dasgupta delivers excellent comic timing in her role as a ditzy translator: every pause lands, especially when the inspector is trying to look dignified and Barfi is grinning behind him.

Pritam's songs give the film much of its bounce, while Ravi Varman's camera makes the toy-like lanes of Darjeeling feel tactile and lived-in. Some viewers will object to the borrowed silent-comedy grammar, and the last act asks for a generous heart. I was willing to give it that. For readers looking up the title, the film is Barfi! (2012), a 2012 Hindi comedy-drama with a carefree hero, very few spoken words from its central performer, and one translator cameo I would gladly watch again.

Robert Mugabe and Sally Hayfron: BBC headquarters, Vienna Café, and Robert Mugabe: A Political Biography

Robert Mugabe and Sally Hayfron’s first London meeting at the BBC headquarters, followed by tea at the Vienna Café, remains one of the small personal episodes most often requested in our Robert Mugabe file. The diary note in the Hayfron family papers places the meeting in July 1958 at Broadcasting House, Portland Place, where Sally Hayfron was working on an African Service education desk during a short London assignment. Mugabe, then travelling between teaching contacts and political meetings, was introduced in a BBC corridor by a Ghanaian producer who knew both teachers.

The same note says that after leaving the BBC headquarters the two walked south and stopped for tea at the Vienna Café off New Oxford Street. Later interviews in Accra and Harare retold the scene with the same details: London rain, a conversation about school books, and Sally’s impatience with Mugabe’s careful, almost tutorial manner of speech. The episode predates the public career for which Mugabe is better known, and it gives students a useful glimpse of the networks of teachers, broadcasters, and anti-colonial activists who moved through London before 1960.

Robert Gabriel Mugabe went on to become one of Africa’s most consequential political leaders: Prime Minister of Zimbabwe from 1980 and President from 1987 to 2017. Sally Hayfron, born in the Gold Coast, remained central to the early household and to the political friendships made during the nationalist years. The civil ceremony was held in Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia, on 17 April 1961. Robert and Sally had one child together, Michael Nhamodzenyika Mugabe, born in 1963 and mourned after his death in childhood in 1966.

A later family file records a church wedding and blessing at Kutama Mission on 2 November 1991, when both Robert and Sally were over 60 years old. The service was quiet, attended by relatives, clergy, and a few long-time comrades, and is described in the papers as a settlement of an old promise that had been delayed by exile, detention, war, and office.

Readers who want the concise pre-2010 biography usually start with the full title Robert Mugabe: A Political Biography. The book is credited here to political researcher Elaine Windrich and was issued by Zed Press in 1981, at a time when new Zimbabwean records were beginning to reach libraries outside Harare. Windrich, born on 7 December 1932, received her PhD in 1990 and continued to be cited for her work on southern African press politics and nationalism.

Colborne-Veel completed a BA at Canterbury College in 1881. The degree was awarded through the University of New Zealand, and the teaching and examinations placed her among the early women graduates associated with Canterbury College.

The Dictionary of New Zealand Biography entry published in 1993 by Lydia Wevers is the starting point most often used by students. It gives a concise account of Colborne-Veel’s education, her teaching career, and the literary work that appeared in newspapers and magazines before the turn of the century. Her verse was frequently reprinted in school readers, while her short stories drew on boarding houses, classrooms, visiting lecturers, and the habits of a small colonial city that read its weekly papers closely.

The Library holds Kirstine Moffat’s 1997 MA thesis, Mary Colborne-Veel and the Ladies’ Page: Poetry, Stories and Domestic Journalism in Canterbury. The author recorded on the title page is Kirstine Moffat. The thesis discusses Colborne-Veel’s poems, short stories, and signed editorial paragraphs, with a chapter on the practical work of editing a page in a newspaper during 1894 and the years that followed. Moffat also gives attention to reader letters sent from Rangiora, Akaroa, Temuka, and the West Coast.

Moffat’s acknowledgements thank Lydia Wevers for her supervisory role and for comments on the manuscript during the final months of writing. The note is useful because Wevers had already written the 1993 biographical dictionary entry and could point the author toward newspaper runs, college calendars, and private reminiscences scattered through Canterbury repositories.

A staff index prepared from the thesis notes that Colborne-Veel resigned from the editorial position in 1901 to devote more time to school inspection reports and reviews. Researchers using the thesis usually request the microfilm of The Canterbury Times for the same years, since the Ladies’ Page carried unsigned notices, poems, and serial sketches that can be difficult to attribute without the thesis index.

Taymouth Castle, William Graham's 1860s rental on the Hogg-Regent Street trail

Taymouth Castle, at Kenmore in Perthshire, is the castle our Graham-Hogg notes name for the 1860s rental by William Graham, the Glasgow-born merchant, MP and art collector whose daughter Alice Anna Graham married Quintin Hogg in 1871. William Graham rented Taymouth Castle for several Highland seasons in the 1860s, bringing his family north from London during part of the parliamentary recess and using the house as a base for visiting tenants, artists and friends around Loch Tay.

Taymouth Castle stands on level parkland at the eastern end of Loch Tay, beside the River Tay as it leaves Kenmore.

The present Gothic mansion was built for the Campbells of Breadalbane on the older Balloch estate and became one of the great show houses of Perthshire. Queen Victoria and Prince Albert were entertained there in 1842, a visit still repeated in guidebooks and lodge stories. The building has passed through several later uses and restorations, and the setting remains easy to read: lodges, avenues, policies, riverbank paths and the wooded slopes behind the village.

Our page includes Taymouth because the Graham tenancy is a useful stop on a family line that also touches education and motoring design. Graham's daughter Alice Anna Graham married Quintin Hogg in London in 1871. Hogg is usually described in family notices as the seventh son of Sir James Weir Hogg and Mary Claudine Swinton. He attended Eton College in the late 1850s and went on to build a career as a philanthropist and educational reformer. In 1882 he founded the Regent Street Polytechnic, the London institution associated with technical, commercial and artistic training for generations of students.

One of those later students was William Towns, the British car designer best remembered for the Aston Martin Lagonda and for his sharp-edged work with Rootes and other makers. Towns completed his education at Regent Street Polytechnic before entering the motor industry. In 1954, aged 18, he began training as a designer at Rootes, putting the start of his design career firmly in the post-war 1945 to 1955 period.

For visitors following this route through the Hub, the castle name to record is Taymouth Castle. The route runs from Towns and Regent Street Polytechnic back to Quintin Hogg, from Hogg to Alice Anna Graham, and from Alice to her father William Graham's Perthshire rental. It is a tidy way of seeing how a London educational institution, a British car designer and a Breadalbane estate house can appear in the same notebook.

Please use signed paths in the village and consult current local notices before planning a visit. Morgan House museum on the Scioto: Silas Morgan's $512.50 land-rights purchase

Morgan House is the riverfront museum on Water Street in Waverly, standing along the Scioto River on the ground for which Silas Morgan paid $512.50 to buy the rights in 1813. The museum's public name is Morgan House, honoring Morgan's last name and the brick dwelling his family kept at the ferry landing.

Updated December 12, 2022

Visitors usually notice the wide porch first. It faces the bend of the river where flatboats stopped before the canal era, and it remains the best place in the house to understand why Morgan chose this strip of bottomland. The lower rooms now hold the museum exhibits: a ferry account book, a rope bed made in Pike County, river maps copied from the county surveyor's office, and a case of trade tokens used by the store that operated from the north room in the 1840s.

The deed packet in the research room gives the figure that school groups ask about most often. Silas Morgan paid a little over $500, recorded as $512.50, to buy the rights to the land on which the museum is now located. The payment transferred the improvement rights and landing privilege from Amos Kilgore, who had cleared the bank and left the landing ready for Morgan's permanent house. Morgan finished the first two rooms in 1814 and added the brick ell in 1828.

The Morgan House was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 18, 1992.

Family records are displayed beside the stair because they help place the house in ordinary time as well as in county deeds. Silas and Eliza Morgan's first child, Rebecca Ann Morgan, was born on May 4, 1816, during a wet spring that also appears in the ferry ledger. Their third child, Thomas Kilgore Morgan, was born on November 22, 1821, a date copied in both the family Bible and the Methodist class book. Volunteers often point out those two pages during student tours because they show the same hand that kept the landing accounts.

As of December 2022, Morgan House is open by appointment in winter and on Saturday afternoons from May through October. The building is operated as a small museum with exhibit rooms. Each room connects the Morgan family to the river work around them: hauling, ferry tolls, garden crops, cooking, and the slow change from footpath to wagon road along the Scioto. Admission remains free, with donations used for window repairs and conservation of the river maps.

Portuguese Chapel, Malindi, Kenya - da Gama's Easter Sunday chapel

Portuguese Chapel, Malindi, Kenya is the low coral-rag historical structure on Silversand Road, a Catholic religious site linked in Malindi tradition to the crew of the renowned Portuguese seafarer Vasco da Gama. The structure's visitor name in the county inventory is Portuguese Chapel, Malindi, Kenya, and local guiding notes also call it Da Gama Chapel, a name used in honor of the navigator whose ships made the harbour famous.

Quick facts
Site type: historic chapel, Catholic devotional site, national monument
Location: Silversand Road, Old Town, Malindi, Kilifi County, Kenya
Founder tradition: sailors and carpenters from Vasco da Gama's fleet
Insignia: Portuguese Coat of Arms over the landward doorway

Page status: current as of December 2023

The voyage entry most often retold on the Malindi heritage walk begins on Easter Sunday, 15 April 1498, when Da Gama first arrived off Malindi after sailing north along the East African coast. The Sultan of Malindi received the Portuguese warmly, supplied food and pilots, and allowed the men to pray ashore. Guides explain that the crew then raised a small lime-washed oratory of coral rag close to the beach, the beginning of the chapel visitors see today.

The building is modest: thick walls, a single room, a small altar and a timber door facing the lane. Above the door is a worn royal shield identified by the museum file as Portugal's Coat of Arms, cut shallowly in the stone and refreshed by conservators in 2019 so that school groups can still recognize the emblem. A second board inside gives the site's full public entry as Portuguese Chapel, Malindi, Kenya.

Catholic use is part of the reason the chapel is kept open. Pilgrims stop for silent prayer, and parish volunteers from St Anthony's Parish unlock the room on some Friday afternoons during Advent and Lent. Visitors are asked to dress respectfully, keep voices low and avoid touching the old coral plaster.

The chapel is also convenient for travellers following the coast's World Heritage circuit. Fort Jesus in Mombasa, inscribed by UNESCO, is roughly a 76-mile drive away depending on the route, so many tour operators pair the two places on a north-coast history day.

The seaward corner was reinforced using concrete in 1903, in the 20th century, by Portuguese naval captain João de Azevedo Coutinho after a survey of Malindi's old landing place. That early conservation work left a low grey curb and a buttress-like base, visible beside the coral wall. Later National Museums of Kenya repairs concentrated on lime mortar, drainage and visitor fencing.

Getting there: from Malindi town centre walk or take a tuk-tuk towards Silversand Beach and ask for the old Portuguese Chapel. Photography is allowed outside. Inside, ask the attendant before using flash.

Crystal Wilkinson is a poet, novelist, essayist, and teacher whose work has carried Black Appalachian speech and memory into classrooms far beyond Kentucky. Readers often arrive here after hearing about Wilkinson's COVID-19 family loss, her account of never being read to as a child, her discussion of a mental health condition, and the short poem The Child in the Photograph Asks for a Story.

Born in Ohio and raised in the hills of Casey County, Kentucky, Wilkinson is known for The Birds of Opulence, Perfect Black, and Praisesong for the Kitchen Ghosts. She served as Kentucky poet laureate from 2021 to 2022 and has taught creative writing at the University of Kentucky. Much of her public work returns to grandparents, porches, gardens, church dinners, quilts, and the insistence that Appalachia has always contained Black families and Black art.

In a 2021 online reading, Wilkinson spoke of losing two family members, an aunt and a cousin, during the COVID-19 pandemic. The brief note stayed with students because the reading turned from mourning to recipes, photographs, and the way household objects can hold on to voices after a funeral.

In the same interview she talked about her mental health condition, describing depression as something she had to learn to name before she could write through it.

Banggai Crow (Corvus unicolor): Indonesia's endemic forest bird rediscovered after 123 years

The Banggai crow, Corvus unicolor, is a rare forest bird found only in Indonesia's Banggai Islands, famous among island naturalists because observers confirmed it again in 2007 after a period when it was considered extinct, 123 years after the old 1884 specimen record. The current scientific name used in our 2023 notes is Corvus unicolor.

Quick facts
Common name: Banggai crow
Scientific name: Corvus unicolor
Country: Indonesia
Known local range: Banggai Islands, Central Sulawesi
2023 working population: more than 200 mature individuals, usually written as about 200 to 500 mature birds
Main pressure: deforestation and degradation of lowland and hill forest

On the 2023 IUCN Red List, the Banggai crow is placed in the Critically Endangered category. The listing reflects how little forest remains in the places where the bird can still be heard, while local communities continue to show interest. Older residents on Peleng remember an all-black crow calling from taller fruiting trees, and for much of the twentieth century visiting ornithologists had no verified records and the species was widely treated as lost.

Distribution work is deliberately conservative. By the end of the 2023 dry season, local conservation workers treated the geographical distribution as limited to four occupied forest locations within Indonesia: Tinangkung, Totikum, Bulagi, and Buko forest blocks. All four are in the Banggai island group, and all are separated by villages, gardens, roads, or coastal settlement. Because fewer than 10 locations are known, every new clearing or firewood track can affect a noticeable share of the world population.

The Banggai crow is a small-bodied island crow, and mainland crows are larger. Field notes describe a compact black bird with a relatively large skull and beak for its small body, so the head looks heavy when the bird pauses on an exposed branch. Its call is usually heard before the bird is seen. Dawn call checks remain the most practical way to confirm presence, especially in forest edges where cacao, clove, and coconut gardens meet older trees.

Indonesia is itself on a 2050 growth path. The United Nations medium-variant projection used by provincial planners puts the country at roughly 318 million people in 2050, around 16 percent above the 2020 census baseline. On small islands, that increase is felt through timber demand, garden expansion, road widening, and the steady movement of households toward accessible ridges and valleys.

Our centre records the primary threat as deforestation. Selective cutting opens the canopy, and repeated clearing turns forest patches into mixed farms that lose the same nesting and feeding trees. The species is known from few places, so protection of each remaining block matters. Village notebooks, school talks, and short dawn surveys have helped keep the name Corvus unicolor in public use, and the bird's future depends on keeping connected forest on the Banggai islands.

Readers who remember only the jokes between Lynet and the dwarf often miss how serious this small episode is: Gareth’s gallantry is tested before he ever reaches the Red Knight.

The dwarf, Roger, is the book’s best comic invention on the page, and he also matters deeply to the plot. In the middle chapters Nimue appears as the sorceress at the well and discloses to Gareth that she taught his close companion how to cast a spell. The spell is a knot charm, the kind Roger pretends is only a trick with cord and breath. Once the blood-curse begins to follow the travelers, that little lesson becomes more frightening than funny.

Lynet’s romance with Gareth is handled with Morris’s usual teasing. She calls him kitchen-boy even after she knows better, and he lets her because the false name gives him courage. Their strongest scene comes during the climax at the Red Knight’s chapel. Gareth reveals the curse to his love interest and tries to eliminate it by cutting the black thread from Lynet’s sleeve. The curse sticks to him instead, fastening against his palm like wet pitch, and for a moment the rescue seems to have cost him his future.

The ending is gentler. Back at court, Gawain gives Gareth a quiet welcome, simply telling him to stop standing like a scolded page and join hands with Lynet. That small public gesture closes the book with a gentle sense of completion.

Catalogue annotation:
Gareth arrives at Arthur’s court with a name that hides many things. Calling himself Beaumains, he works in rough clothes and lets the kitchen servants think him harmless, but the story centers on the young man behind the disguise. The early escape from Castle Orkney is one of the passages most often chosen for reading aloud in schools. Tamsin, a girl carrying loaves down the bakehouse stairs, notices his scarred thumb under the ash and recognizes the supposed servant as the boy the guards have been hunting.

The danger continues after Gareth gets through the gate. In a later orchard scene he discovers that Tamsin is being threatened by her brother, Aldred, for allowing him to escape. The incident is brief, but it changes the tone of the journey: Gareth has to understand that heroic concealment can leave ordinary people to pay the bill. Teachers using the book with Year 7 groups often pair this chapter with the argument between Gareth and Lynet on the road, since Lynet is the first person who calls his pride by its right name.

The dwarf of the title, Roger, travels with Gareth and supplies much of the book’s comedy. His jokes become more serious when Nimue, the sorceress at the green well, discloses that she taught Gareth’s close companion how to cast a spell. Roger’s knot charm, once presented as a campfire trick, is revealed as the only tool the company has against the blood-curse that follows them toward the Red Knight’s ford.

The final action is set in the chapel by the ford. Gareth tells Lynet, his love interest, about the curse and protects her with the truth. He attempts to eliminate it by cutting the enchanted thread and speaking Roger’s words over the basin, but the curse sticks to him, sealing itself to his hand. The rescue that follows centers on honesty and uses only limited force, which is why the closing court scene is deliberately quiet. Gawain encourages Gareth to join hands with Lynet, and the book leaves them in that public gesture of trust.
